Adobe (ADBE -2.90%) has a new Sell rating to deal with. On Nov. 4, Citigroup analyst Tyler Radke downgraded the creative software company to Sell from Neutral and cut his price target to $207 from $250. Citi sees downside risk to Wall Street's growth estimates for Adobe going into fiscal 2027.
Shares didn't drop on the news. Actually, Adobe stock gained about 1% that day.
But the stock was already having a tough year. At roughly $242 as I write, it's down about 31% in 2026.
I wrote about Adobe's long history of steep drops under two weeks ago, and Citi's Sell rating is the only new development since then. I don't think the downgrade is wrong about the direction of Adobe's growth. But I do think the stock price already bakes in something far worse than what Adobe's own numbers show.
Image source: Getty Images.
Adobe's growth is slowing
Citi points to industry data showing rising pressure on Adobe from artificial intelligence (AI) and among small businesses. It also thinks changes to the creative business under Anil Chakravarthy, who becomes Adobe's CEO on Dec. 1, might hold back short-term growth.
Adobe's own numbers already show some slowing. Heading into fiscal 2026, the company aimed for 10.2% growth in total annualized recurring revenue (ARR), a gauge of what its subscriptions pull in over a year. Later, Adobe closed its acquisition of the marketing software company Semrush, which added around $480 million in ARR. But the full-year ARR target didn't move. Without the purchase, that target comes out to growth of only around 8%.
Profits are cooling, too. Adobe's non-GAAP (adjusted) net income climbed around 8% year over year in the fiscal third quarter of 2026 (the period ended Aug. 28, 2026), down from about 11% in the fiscal second quarter and 12% in fiscal Q1. Revenue, of course, still rose 13% from a year earlier to a record $6.76 billion in fiscal Q3.
And if the slowdown in profit growth persists into fiscal 2027, Citi's concern about next year's estimates could prove right.
A higher earnings target
Earnings per share look stronger, mainly because Adobe continues to buy back its stock. Showing how much the buyback matters, the company's diluted share count shrank around 7% year over year in fiscal Q3, to 395 million. So adjusted earnings per share climbed 15% that quarter, almost twice the growth in adjusted net income.
Management has lifted its full-year earnings goal along the way, too. In December, Adobe's fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings per share target indicated growth of around 12% over fiscal 2025's $20.94. After two hikes, the latest target of $24.45 to $24.50 implies growth of around 17%.
Sure, buybacks can't hide a shrinking business forever. But Adobe isn't shrinking. Management's revenue goal for fiscal 2026 is around $26.6 billion, about 12% above the $23.8 billion Adobe took in during fiscal 2025.
Also, the company still generates billions of dollars in operating cash flow every quarter, which helps fund those buybacks. Operating cash flow was about $2.5 billion in fiscal Q3 alone.
Time to buy?

Days after voters ousted all three Republican justices on the 15th Court of Appeals in Tuesday’s election, the court canceled oral arguments for four cases, telling lawyers the case will be reset “at a later date.”
The change will leave the cases — including a challenge to state rules limiting the sale of hemp-derived products containing THC — to three Democrats who will take office in early January.
The THC regulations, originally set to take effect at the end of March, included child-resistant packaging, a significant increase in licensing fees, new labeling, testing and bookkeeping requirements. The Texas Department of State Health Services rules also codified the legal purchasing age to 21 and increased licensing fees for manufacturers of hemp-derived THC from $258 to $10,000 per facility and retail registrations from $155 to $5,000. Industry leaders said the fees amounted to a ban by forcing businesses to close.
Smoke shops briefly pulled the products from shelves as the ban went into effect before a Travis County district judge on April 10 temporarily blocked the rules as a lawsuit by the hemp industry played out in court.
The 15th Court of Appeals, which has statewide jurisdiction over challenges to state laws and regulations, was set to hear oral arguments in the case Dec. 8.
The cancellation will let current justices deliver opinions on already argued cases, Justice Scott Field told Bloomberg Law.
“We know we can’t get the opinion out for cases orally argued before the end of the year so we don’t want to waste the lawyers’ time with an argument if there’s a chance the new court will also want to hear argument,” Field said.
There are 39 cases before the outgoing justices that have already presented oral or written arguments and are awaiting opinions.
Oral arguments set for Dec. 8 and 9 also were canceled in:
• The State of Texas vs. Sunrise Community Church Inc., a legal battle around a homeless shelter in South Austin. The attorney general’s office argued the shelter’s proximity to an elementary school makes it a public nuisance.
• Comptroller Don Huffines and Attorney General Ken Paxton vs. City of Lancaster, a dispute over about $3 million in sales taxes.
• Huffines and Paxton vs. Dave & Buster’s, which sued to recover $2.58 million that the company believed qualified for tax exemptions.

The spirit of the fall marathon is undeniably contagious: the roaring crowds, the crisp autumn air, and massive community energy. If you spectated this year, watching the hundreds (if not thousands) of runners race toward the finish line might have you yearning to lace up your shoes and hit the starting line next season. But before you jump into training, hit pause and make sure you’re prepared for success.
“Training to run a marathon will revolutionize your life, but it will also test you in brand-new ways,” says Susie Crossland-Dwyer, an avid marathoner and ultramarathoner, coach, and founder of studio s in Cincinnati. “A lot goes into a healthy, successful training season and what you do leading up to it.”
Here are nine tips that coaches want every marathoner to know to get to race day healthy, strong, and fast!
1. Make Sure You Have an Adequate Base
You’re about to set out on four-plus months of intense weekly mileage. That’s really tough on your body. To sidestep an overuse injury, having a steady foundation is crucial. A review of research on runners’ injuries published in the Journal of Sport and Health Science found that the injury incidence rate among runners is 40.2 percent, and overuse from ramping up mileage or intensity too quickly causes more than 70 percent of the injuries.
“As you begin your marathon season, start with base building and don’t just jump right into doing all the miles and all the speed workouts,” advises Crossland-Dwyer, who recommends spending at least three months gradually working up to 20 to 25 miles per week before starting an official marathon training program.
2. Start Resistance Workouts
“Strength training, specifically your core and hips, is the most effective way to prevent injuries,” says Jeff Gaudette, owner and head coach at RunnersConnect. “As you ramp up your mileage for the marathon, this will be essential to you staying healthy through the training segment.”
Studies have found that strength training can also boost your performance by improving your running economy. You don’t need a certain base of strength before starting your training plan, he says, but you should include two to three weight workouts each week.
Along with weight training, “try plyometrics to get your body used to absorbing impact, single-leg exercises to prevent muscle imbalances, and mobility drills to keep your range of motion and joints healthy,” advises Meg Takacs, NASM-CPT, a run coach and founder of the Movement & Miles app.
3. Figure Out a Fueling Plan
Carb-loading before race day is what most novice runners are familiar with when starting on their marathon-training journey, but it’s only one aspect of your diet that’s important.
“Nutrition is key for successful training and a successful race—from carbs to water, electrolytes, and salt capsules,” says Takacs. “The goal is to stay ahead of any deficits before they happen because once you’re in a hydration or nutritional deficit, it’s almost impossible to come back.”
Buy water bottles to carry with you on long runs (sip water or a sports drink every 10 to 15 minutes), plus gels or gummies to nibble on every 30 minutes to stay fueled and strong through your long runs ahead.
4. Be Realistic About Training Time
We’re not talking about the race itself—though, yes, you’re going to be on your feet for a long time for that, too. But it’s important to know the kind of time commitment you’re going to be looking at for the next 16 or so weeks leading up to race day.

What is Implied Volatility?
Implied volatility shows how much movement the market is expecting in the future. Options with high levels of implied volatility suggest that investors in the underlying stocks are expecting a big move in one direction or the other. It could also mean there is an event coming up soon that may cause a big rally or a huge sell-off. However, implied volatility is only one piece of the puzzle when putting together an options trading strategy.
What do the Analysts Think?

- SpaceX rose 5% today after Stifel argued it could buy stalled data center sites that already have power.
- Permitting fights after the midterms should hurt developers awaiting approvals more than SpaceX.

SpaceX (SPCX) is up 5% today after Stifel analyst Jonathan Siegmann argued the data center backlash after the Democrats’ midterm sweep could work in its favor. With an investment-grade balance sheet and $40 billion of committed GPU financing, he wrote, SpaceX is “positioned as buyer of last resort for sites that already have power.” He kept his Buy rating and $190 price target.
He’s not alone. Applied Digital (APLD) CEO Wes Cummins made the same case for his campuses in the company’s Oct. 7 earnings release: “we view every new restriction elsewhere as making what we already own harder to replicate.”
Permits are the new bottleneck
Siegmann expects the friction to hit projects planned for 2028, rather than sites already under construction. Texas is the flashpoint: Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned on a moratorium on new data centers, and Wells Fargo puts 27% of planned US data center gigawatts in the state. P&G also challenged claims that the product nourishes the driest skin, as well as the product name "Deep Moisture."
The 24-Hour Claims
Unilever supported its 24-hour moisturization claims with a short-term moisturization study (STM Study) designed to measure skin hydration over 24 hours following a single wash with Dove Deep Moisture Body Wash. NAD found that Unilever's STM Study is an appropriate study to measure moisture on the skin. P&G submitted studies challenging the STM Study, but NAD concluded that P&G had not shown Unilever's STM Study was flawed or that its own studies were more reliable. NAD therefore found Unilever's evidence sufficient to support its claims that Dove Deep Moisture Body Wash moisturizes skin for 24 hours and provides continued moisture renewal and regeneration.
The "Round-the-Clock" Claim
P&G also challenged the "round-the-clock deep moisture" claim, arguing that it conveys significant moisturizing benefits for an extended period after in-shower use. NAD found that, because the claim appears above language stating that the product "restores moisture for 24 hours," consumers could reasonably understand it to promise 24-hour moisturization. Having found the 24-hour claims supported, NAD determined that the round-the-clock claim was also supported.

Federal officials announced rural health grants to states (David DeWitt/Ohio Capital Journal).
Federal officials on Monday announced $10 billion in awards across all 50 states in the second year of the Rural Health Transformation Fund, grants created by Congress to bolster rural health in response to concerns about Medicaid cuts.
That includes $218 million for Missouri.
Texas received the largest grant for the 2027 fiscal year — almost $282 million — followed by Alaska, Montana, California and Oklahoma.
The five-year fund is providing $50 billion in grants meant to address rural healthcare access and health improvement, with $10 billion available each year until 2030.
Congress created the program in response to concern from rural health care providers — as well as lawmakers on both sides of the aisle — about the effects of sweeping Medicaid cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that President Donald Trump signed last year. Rural areas are expected to lose about $137 billion, according to health research organization, KFF.
Half of the annual funding is distributed equally among states, with each receiving $100 million in “baseline” funds. The other half is calculated based on a state’s rural population and healthcare facilities, as well as specific initiatives detailed in the applications, among other factors.
States applied for and developed their own programs, using the money toward focus areas ranging from maternal and behavioral health, preventive health and chronic disease management, access to care and the rural healthcare workforce, and tech and health equipment investments.
All 50 states submitted annual reports documenting their progress from the first year. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said it reviewed the reports as part of determining each state’s award for this year.
“States have already put these resources to work bringing better care closer to home for their rural communities, and CMS looks forward to helping them build on that progress in the coming year,” agency Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz said in a news release.
States must use the grants to test out and grow approaches toward making programs sustainable after the fund’s five years have ended, the agency said.
Rural healthcare leaders have said the infusion of federal dollars is welcome but won’t be enough to offset Medicaid cuts. Democrats, who won the majority in both the U.S. House and Senate in this month’s midterm elections, are aiming to push for a repeal of the law, which would still need Trump’s signature.

“I’ve always had to feel like I needed to be good in every area of the game,” Wetherholt said. “I’ve never had crazy tools, so I just wanted to make sure that all those tools are out to play, especially in the big leagues.”
Those tools certainly played in 2026, a standout rookie season for the Cardinals second baseman. Wetherholt officially finished third in National League Rookie of the Year Award voting, as announced Monday night on MLB Network. Reds infielder Sal Stewart won the award, while Mets outfielder Carson Benge was the runner-up.
Wetherholt earned 99 voting points, receiving three of 30 possible first-place votes as well as 12 second-place votes, six third-place votes, five fourth-place votes and two fifth-place votes. He was vying to become the seventh Rookie of the Year in franchise history and the first since Albert Pujols in 2001.
The 24-year-old was MLB Pipeline’s No. 5 overall prospect when he made the Cardinals’ 2026 Opening Day roster, earning an everyday job and running with it. He posted a .242/.339/.365 slash line, slugging 17 home runs and stealing 14 bases in 15 attempts. Wetherholt showed impressive plate discipline as a rookie, striking out just 16.8% of the time (in the 77th percentile of MLB hitters) and walking just 10.3% of the time. He was St. Louis’ regular leadoff man, batting first in all 135 of his starts.
Not only was Wetherholt a hair above average as a hitter (he had a 102 OPS+ as a rookie), but his glove was the best at his position and among the best anywhere in the Majors. Wetherholt recorded a +23 fielding run value and +25 outs above average, ranking second in each category behind Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong (+26 in each).
Wetherholt made 131 appearances at second base and just 12 at shortstop, a marked change from 2025 in the Minor Leagues, when he played mostly short while seeing occasional time at both second and third base.
“It was a ton of fun this year just growing at second base, a position that I played for most of my life,” Wetherholt said.
Born in Baltimore, Wetherholt was raised in western Pennsylvania and attended Mars Area High School, the same school as current free-agent closer David Bednar. He committed to play at West Virginia and spent 2022-24 with the Mountaineers, batting an impressive .449 as a sophomore in ’23 and finishing his collegiate career with a .370 batting average and 29 home runs.
Selected seventh overall by the Cardinals in the 2024 Draft, Wetherholt appeared in 29 games for Single-A Palm Beach that year before splitting time between Double-A and Triple-A in 2025. In 138 career Minor League games, Wetherholt posted a .304/.418/.487 slash line.
That kind of offensive production coupled with a solid Spring Training was enough to earn Wetherholt an early ticket to the big leagues. “Just was out there having fun, trying to be competitive out there, and I was able to put a good year together,” Wetherholt said.

ExxonMobil (XOM -0.69%) and Chevron (CVX -0.86%) are two of the world's largest energy companies. Their share prices are high today because energy prices are high today. If history is any guide, neither of those situations will last forever. But the really important thing to understand about these two companies is that they are built to survive the entire energy cycle while still rewarding investors with dividends. Here's what you need to know.
Energy prices will eventually fall and take Exxon and Chevron with them
Exxon and Chevron are what are known as integrated energy companies. That means that they have operations across the entire energy sector, from the upstream (drilling) through the midstream (pipelines) and to the downstream (chemicals and refining). That diversification is meant to help soften the impact of commodity price swings.
That said, these two energy giants remain heavily dependent on commodity prices for their revenues and earnings. When oil prices are high, they do well; when they're low, they don't do as well and can even lose money. Energy is a commodity with a long history of volatility, rising and falling in response to supply and demand, natural and man-made disasters, and geopolitical conflicts, among other things. Right now, oil prices are high due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.
History is very clear: at some point the conflict will likely end, and oil prices will decline. When that happens, Exxon and Chevron's stock prices will fall. In fact, if you are patient, the best time to buy one of these companies isn't when energy prices are high, but when they are low. Of course, that requires stepping in to buy when others are selling, which can be difficult.

Exxon and Chevron are built to survive
The thing is, Exxon and Chevron are well aware of the energy cycle and prepared to deal with it. For example, they have debt-to-equity ratios of 0.13x and 0.17x, respectively. They have the lowest leverage in their peer group. This enables the two companies to take on debt during energy downturns, allowing them to continue funding their businesses and supporting their dividends.
Dividends are a key feature here, with Exxon having increased its dividend annually for 43 consecutive years. Chevron isn't far behind at 38 years. That's the proof that their diversified business models, built atop rock-solid balance sheets, work. And it is also why these two stocks are always solid picks in the energy sector for dividend-focused investors.

To be fair, the oil downturn during the pandemic was unusually deep. However, oil downturns are very common. So if you can be patient, now might not be the best time to buy Exxon or Chevron. An aging population keeps that tenant list growing, and a handful of real estate investment trusts (REITs) collect the rent. British drugmaker GSK has settled lawsuits that accused Moderna’s COVID-19 vaccines Spikevax and mNEXSPIKE and RSV shot mResvia of infringing its patents, the companies said on Oct. 6.
Moderna said in a press release that it settled GSK’s patent litigation in the US and Europe on October 28 and that the companies “granted patent cross-licenses in the field of infectious disease and are not obligated to make payments of any kind in connection with such licenses.”

GSK sued Moderna in 2024 over lipid nanoparticle technology used in the vaccines to transport fragile messenger RNA (mRNA) into the human body. GSK separately filed a similar lawsuit against Pfizer and BioNTech over their COVID-19 vaccine earlier that year, which is still ongoing.

Flooding on Florida’s east coast last week was so severe that it has caused the indefinite closure of a 90-bed rehabilitation hospital in Melbourne.
Sea Pines Rehabilitation Hospital, owned in part by Alabama-based Encompass Health, sustained substantial damage in the torrential rains that hammered parts of Florida’s east-central coastal areas with as much as 25 inches of rain in one day.
The 70,000-square-foot hospital was able to evacuate all patients before the floodwaters rose. Some were sent home, others went to other area hospitals.
“We are enormously grateful for the heroic efforts of our hospital staff and the first responders in ensuring the safety of our patients during this catastrophic weather event,” Pat Tuer, Encompass Health’s chief operating officer, said in a statement. “Sea Pines has served the greater Melbourne area for more than 40 years, and we are committed to restoring and enhancing our capacity to do so.”
He said that reopening Sea Pines is a high priority, but the company is discussing its options with its joint venture partner, Holmes Regional Medical Center, on the best path forward.
The hospital, on Florida Avenue in Melbourne, showed net operating revenue of $44 million for the first nine months of this year, said Encompass Health. The publicly traded company said it is the largest owner and operator of inpatient rehab hospitals in the country.
While the hospital is shut down, it will incur expenses for repairs and remediation, as well as some operating expenses. Encompass Health noted in the statement that these expenses are not indicative of the company’s overall operating performance and intends to exclude them, as well as any related insurance proceeds, from its adjusted financial results.
The three days of rain and flooding that shuttered the hospital, called a “1-in-1,000-year” event, also resulted in the deaths of two people in the area. Gov. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency for seven counties.

Matthew Martinez has lived nearly all of his 60 years in a canyon on the Navajo River and had never seen severe floods.
Then, twice over the last two weeks, the river surged through his home and outbuildings in far southwestern Colorado, about 25 miles (40 kilometers) south of the resort town of Pagosa Springs. Now a horse is missing, his barn is damaged and the river swallowed a corral. The house is strewn with mud. His tools washed downstream.
“We’re in trouble, all of us are. Not just me, everybody,” Martinez said through tears when he returned Wednesday. He said several families that go back 100 years in the same canyon had similar damage. “Nobody expected this.”
The Navajo, San Juan and Animas rivers are among those that surged beyond their banks when round after round of storms dumped heavy rain across the Four Corners region of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah.
Scientists say a supercharged El Niño event — when warm water in the Pacific disrupts weather patterns — is making heavy rainfall more likely and increasingly intense across the South.
Recent flooding has struck Flagstaff, Sedona and Tucson in Arizona; Pagosa Springs and Durango in southwestern Colorado; Farmington in northwestern New Mexico; tiny Bluff in southeastern Utah; parts of the vast Navajo Nation.
With a break in the weather at last, some evacuees are returning home.
For Martinez, who was out of town for knee surgery, getting back meant navigating a mucky mess with a four-wheel drive vehicle and a lot of patience over beaten gravel roads. And he’s finding his struggles may have just begun.
Martinez said he doesn’t have flood insurance because insurers wouldn’t provide cover for a house so near the water. He estimates at least $200,000 in losses.
He and his fiancée first stayed with one of his sons, then moved to a hotel. Both places subsequently flooded. Now they’re in an Airbnb, but he worries they could end up homeless when his emergency voucher runs out in a few days.
“The government spends, you know, just millions and billions of money on overseas and everything. Right now we need that money on this side,” he said. “We need to get this, you know, all this put back together.”
A FEMA representative came to his property and took photos after the first flood. The second flood hit three days later and was twice as bad, he said.
“I know we’re on some list right now,” Martinez said. “So we’ll listen every day and we’ll see what options we have and go from there.”
As he heals from the knee surgery, he’s considering whether he should ask family and friends for help cleaning up.
Hauling debris to the dump would cost $300 per load and ultimately could total thousands of dollars he does not readily have, he said.
The flooding did help end months of drought in the Four Corners area, but the raging torrents washed away rich topsoil on his land, leaving just sand and rock. Now he wonders how he’ll feed his remaining animals without pasture next year.
“The normal might not ever be normal again,” Martinez said.
Gruver reported from Fort Collins, Colorado.

Social media platforms face a fresh wave of European Union curbs, this time targeting addictive features and artificial intelligence chatbots.
Under a draft of the “Digital Fairness Act” seen by Bloomberg News, companies would be required to give adult users the ability to switch off features that encourage compulsive or excessive use of their services. The measures would also target AI systems that simulate personal relationships to encourage users to continue interacting with them.
The crackdown could affect some of the world’s biggest technology companies, including Meta Platforms Inc., Alphabet Inc.’s Google and ByteDance Ltd.’s TikTok, whose services rely heavily on features designed to encourage prolonged engagement. Firms would risk fines of up to 6% of worldwide annual revenue for failing to comply with the rules, set to be presented Wednesday.
The European Commission has already taken measures to rebuke social media giants for deploying features that keep users glued to their apps. Both Meta and TikTok are being investigated over suspicions of addictive design under the bloc’s content moderation rulebook, the Digital Services Act.
The EU also plans to ask social networks and AI companies to make their platforms “safe by design” as part of a sweeping Kids Act that will also restrict social media use for young teens.
The commission declined to comment on the draft of the DFA.

France has openly pointed the finger at Iran for recent cyberattacks that crippled fridges and created havoc in hundreds of supermarkets across the nation.
“The responsibility for this attack lies with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps,” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on Monday in Paris, in a rare direct attribution of the hacks to a foreign power.
Barrot, who was speaking on the sidelines of an informal G7 ministerial meeting, said he would be seeking retaliatory measures against Iran and has summoned the country’s ambassador about the matter.
“This is the first large-scale cyberattack with an aim of sabotage on the national territory,” Barrot said. “It hurts the nation’s interests and the security of French citizens. We will take sanctions at the European level against all who are responsible” and “we will take any other proportionate and necessary measure to respond to this attack and dissuade those who would like to reproduce it.”
Representatives for Iran’s foreign ministry didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Related: European Supermarkets Rush to Patch Vulnerabilities After Region-Wide Fridge Hack
In parallel, Paris prosecutors said in a statement Monday they have asked an investigative judge with wider probing powers to pursue the case they’d already begun last month. They are also seeking arrest warrants against the head of an Iranian cyber unit affiliated with Iran’s IRGC and his two deputies.
Investigators identified methods for the attack that were characteristic of this offensive cyber unit, according to the prosecutors, who cited the use of Farsi and IP addresses linked to devices located in Iran.
The hacks in France, affecting some 700 supermarkets, were executed through centralized fridge controllers, connected to the internet, which allow contractors to remotely monitor temperatures. Attackers gained access to some of those systems and manipulated their settings, triggering prolonged defrost cycles that caused refrigerators and freezers to heat up.

Altria vs. Philip Morris: Higher Income Now or Faster Dividend Growth?
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Altria (NYSE:MO | MO Price Prediction) and Philip Morris International (NYSE:PM) both reported third-quarter results in October. They pay out almost the same share of earnings: 88.5% for Altria and 87.7% for Philip Morris. Their yields, though, are far apart. Altria yields 5.53%, and Philip Morris yields 2.98%. That gap shows how the market prices a shrinking U.S. cigarette business against global smoke-free growth.
Marlboro Smokers Trade Down While IQOS Keeps Climbing
Altria’s cigarette volumes are still shrinking, just a little more slowly than the industry. Adjusted domestic shipments fell 4%, compared with an estimated 5% industry decline. Part of the help came from smokers switching to cheaper brands. Marlboro’s retail share slipped 1.0 point to 39.5%, and discount brands rose to 34.1% of the category. Management’s answer is Marlboro Cowboy Cut, which it described as “a premium Marlboro option at the right price to retain value-sensitive smokers.” To me, that is a defensive move. In nicotine pouches, on! volume rose 13.3%, but its share of the pouch category fell to 13.5%. Rivals are growing faster.
Philip Morris grew organic revenue 7.1%. Adjusted EPS came in at $2.36, above the $2.3425 consensus. IQOS in-market sales rose 7.1%, VEEV vape shipments jumped 61.6%, and price increases on international cigarettes added 8.9%. CEO Jacek Olczak called it “another excellent quarter.”
Altria Pulls Cash Out While Philip Morris Reinvests
Altria raised its 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $5.66 to $5.74 and added a $1B increase to its buyback program. Operating cash flow of $3.108 billion in the quarter easily covered $1.774 billion in dividends. Some of the earnings increase came from Altria’s stake in beer maker Anheuser-Busch InBev (NYSE:BUD), where equity income rose to $228M from $123M. Altria has no control over that income.
Philip Morris has no buybacks planned. It is using cash to cut its debt ratio toward 2.0x. Smoke-free products already bring in more than 40% of net revenue. Management expects about $13.5 billion in operating cash flow this year to pay for both growth and the dividend.
Fourth Quarter Will Show the Cost of ZYN’s Price Reset
Philip Morris expects its U.S. adjusted operating income to come in around zero or slightly negative in the fourth quarter. ZYN is moving to 20-pouch cans, which bring in about 25% less revenue per pouch. Energy costs tied to the Middle East and disruptions in Ukraine add about one point of drag on growth. I want to see whether higher ZYN volume makes up for the lower price.
For Altria, watch how many smokers keep moving to discount brands. NJOY ACE also still has no return-to-market date.
Which Dividend Profile Fits Retirement Income Goals Best

A bank group led by JPMorgan Chase (NYSE:JPM | JPM Price Prediction) may offer one of the year’s largest discounts to clear buyout debt it got stuck holding. After the close on November 9, 2026, people familiar with the matter said bankers scheduled investor meetings to discuss selling nearly $2 billion of Qualtrics International debt in the high-yield bond market.
Initial talk points to a coupon of at least 8% and a price of about 85 cents on the dollar. Nothing has been launched or priced, and JPMorgan has issued no filing or press release on the sale.
JPMorgan closed at $342.08 that day, up 2.28%, before the report came out. The stock was $342.11 late in after-hours trading, which shows no meaningful reaction.
For shareholders, the question is whether a loss on one stuck buyout matters. JPMorgan carries a $908.51 billion market value.
What JPMorgan’s Qualtrics Sale Actually Covers
The debt financed Qualtrics’ $6.75 billion purchase of Press Ganey Forsta. Qualtrics is private and owned by Silver Lake and, reportedly, the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, so it has no public financials to check.
In March, the plan was a $5.3 billion package: a $3.3 billion leveraged loan and $2 billion of high-yield bonds. On March 17, the banks stopped it after investors objected to Qualtrics’ exposure to the software selloff and fears of AI disruption.
By May 6, the group expected paper losses of more than $500 million and prepared to fund the deal itself. That made it the year’s biggest hung deal. Banks promised to provide the debt but could not sell it, so it sits on their own books and ties up capital.
A reported 11 institutions, including Goldman Sachs (NYSE:GS), Morgan Stanley (NYSE:MS) and UBS (NYSE:UBS), provided bridge financing. On October 15, JPMorgan considered splitting the debt into about $2 billion each of bonds and loans, and the plan for the loan portion remains undisclosed.
How Much This Costs JPMorgan
A coupon is the fixed interest a bond pays on its face value, and selling at a discount means buyers pay less than face value, so the seller takes the gap.
At the indicated price, the bonds would raise about $1.7 billion. Current yield, the annual coupon divided by the price paid, would be about 9.4%, although the final size, price, coupon, and maturity are not set.
The loss estimate covers the whole bank group, and JPMorgan’s share has never been disclosed. For scale, its Commercial & Investment Bank earned $8.2 billion of net income in the third quarter alone. Selling cheaply still makes sense because it locks in a known loss and frees the balance sheet for fee-paying deals.

The price shows how investors now value software buyouts when AI threatens subscription revenue, and if that pressure keeps building, bond buyers could find the extra yield too thin.
Jamie Dimon, chairman and CEO at the time of the October 13, 2026 earnings call, already sounded cautious: “We are tightening up credit a little bit. I think some of the credit terms have gotten a little bit loose.”
A clean sale would tell private-equity sponsors that stuck debt can clear at a price. A weak reception would make banks slower to commit to the next software buyout.

Costs for goods and services rose more than expected in October, providing fresh warning signs for the Federal Reserve in its fight to lower inflation.
The consumer price index, a broad gauge of costs across the U.S. economy, increased a seasonally adjusted 0.4% for the month, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Tuesday. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones had been looking for a 0.3% increase.
Stripping out volatile food and energy, so-called core CPI increased 0.3% against the forecast for a 0.2% gain.
The headline CPI had increased 0.6% in September while core was up 0.3%.
The report comes at a critical juncture for the Federal Reserve as it considers its next interest-rate move. Speaking Tuesday morning in London ahead of the CPI release, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a hot inflation report could push him toward advocating for a half-point increase in December, and specifically said such a hike should be on the table if core CPI was "around 0.3."
Hours later, that's exactly what happened.
Traders are now fully pricing in a quarter percentage-point increase when the Fed next meets Dec. 8-9, and put odds of a half-point hike at 13.6%, after being around zero prior to the inflation report, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.
Stocks fell following the release, while Treasury yields jumped.
"This was the report the market could least afford to see," said Karen Manna, fixed income investment strategist at Federated Hermes. "A hotter inflation print raises fresh questions about whether the Fed has done enough to contain price pressures and reinforces the risk that interest rates need to move higher and stay there for longer."
The BLS did not estimate a yearly rate in its October inflation report. The government shutdown last year prevented the bureau from collecting sufficient data in October 2025, so there is no comparable figure to use. However, the report did include annual figures for some individual items where it was able to collect data.
Though gasoline prices have been falling in recent weeks, the energy index rose 0.7% and the gasoline index was up 1%. The natural gas index, though, was off 0.8%.

Shelter costs were higher by 0.3%, which the BLS said accounted for more than 30% of the headline increase.
Apparel, a tariff-sensitive sector, rose just 0.1%. Medical care commodities prices increased 0.5%. Airline fares accelerated 0.4%.
At the Fed's October meeting, central bank officials voted 10-2 to keep their benchmark rate in a range between 3.75%-4% while awaiting incoming data.

After a Tyson Foods meatpacking plant closed in Nebraska in January, eliminating about 3,000 jobs, the state secured a temporary reprieve from new Medicaid work requirements for residents of the surrounding county.

Six of the eight states bordering Missouri — Nebraska, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Tennessee, Kentucky and Illinois — plan to offer short-term hardship exceptions.

U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth listens to question during a news conference at the Pentagon on March 2, 2026 in Arlington, Virginia. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth struck a defiant tone Tuesday as he faces potential impeachment by the U.S. House of Representatives this week, casting the effort as an attack on American service members.
Hegseth during a rare news conference at the Pentagon called the impeachment effort a “farce” and flatly rejected the notion that he had committed impeachable offenses as the top civilian leader of the military. He likened himself to President Donald Trump, who was twice impeached during his first term.
“Let’s be clear about what this resolution actually does. It tells our enemies — Iran, the cartels, every adversary watching — that the United States will actually punish its own warriors and its own civilian leadership for successfully executing lawful military operations,” Hegseth said.
The House, led by Republicans during the lame-duck session following the Nov. 3 election, is set to vote on impeaching Hegseth as soon as Wednesday, with a procedural vote expected later Tuesday.
Massie impeachment articles
Rep. Thomas Massie, an outgoing Kentucky Republican, introduced articles of impeachment Monday alleging the defense secretary waged unlawful war against Iran, ordered extrajudicial killings and ignored laws intended to minimize civilian casualties, among other charges.
Impeachment would represent an extraordinary rebuke of one of the most divisive members of Trump’s Cabinet. Democrats, as well as some Republicans, are expected to support the effort, raising the possibility the articles will pass and trigger a trial in the Senate, though the outcome is unclear there.
Hegseth, a 46-year-old former Fox News personality who narrowly won Senate confirmation last year, has sought to project a swashbuckling, masculine image as the military’s top civilian leader. He has rebranded the Department of Defense as the “Department of War,” purged numerous high-ranking officers and tried to kick critical media outlets out of the Pentagon.
On Tuesday, Hegseth called Massie a “disgruntled and defeated congressman” who is attempting a “political spectacle” driven by ego and resentment. Massie, who has often clashed with Trump, lost his primary in May to a Trump-backed challenger.
“It’s a farce and it’s a stunt and everybody knows it,” Hegseth said.
Drug boats

SpaceX plans to construct, own and operate a gas-fired power plant and super-compute facility at its company town in Starbase, Texas, according to a notice of a public hearing on the city’s website.
The estimated investment for the initial phase of the project is $24 billion. The city commissioner will consider the approval of a tax abatement and development agreement at a Dec. 9 meeting.
The proposal is the latest sign that CEO Elon Musk is seeking to vertically integrate SpaceX’s value chain for natural gas, the primary power-plant fuel that data center developers are using to get the facilities up and running. SpaceX is also looking to fuel some of its rocket launches with a super-chilled and purified form of the gas.
In September, SpaceX proposed building its own pipeline in Florida to transport gas to its Starship rockets in Cape Canaveral. The company has also been hiring gas traders in Starbase and Cape Canaveral to support its growing fuel and power needs, rather than relying on external logistics companies.
Starbase, incorporated in 2025, is home to several hundred SpaceX employees and their families. The proposed project is located within the corporate limits of Starbase on a 444-acre tract east of the city of Brownsville, according to the public notice.
Surging power needs from data centers and new factories have driven demand for gas plants, and Musk has long been a proponent for vertical integration. SpaceX also plans to build its own gas-fired power plant to support the massive semiconductor manufacturing facility it’s developing in Grimes County, outside of Houston, with Tesla Inc.
Musk’s prospects for getting a “super-compute facility” and associated gas infrastructure online could face headwinds from Texas’ incoming Democratic governor Gina Hinojosa, who ran in part on a promise to tame new data center construction.
